name: Umar Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Anything you say here is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a trainee excavator operator at the Kanyon Flats lithium mine, a big open pit that's grown like crazy because of the battery boom. I load haul trucks with a 120-tonne excavator, so I'm sitting at the face, swinging, digging, dumping into the truck tray, about four passes a truck. Day shift starts at six with the pre-start and the toolbox talk, then I'm digging till six at night with a half-hour lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the precision. When you load a truck in four clean passes and it's sitting level, that's satisfying. What wears me out is that I'm still not quick, my cycle times are slower than everyone else's, and the shift boss, Hamid, puts the numbers up on the board every week. I've started recording my own cycles and running them through an AI tool at night to see where I'm wasting seconds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, so we got some better tools and the bubble popped. Online I'd probably post a chart about it, I'm that guy. At work nobody would care much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit let down, because I've bet on this. I've got shares in two automation companies and a bit in a mining equipment maker. But my job's safe for longer, so it evens out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do now: dig, use the AI tool to cut my cycle times, and put a chunk of pay into shares every month. I'd still apply to the autonomy project team when it opens, because I want to be near the tech whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your money situation, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About nine months of costs in cash, plus the shares, which are worth about another year if I sold them. I live alone in a small flat in town, the rent's low, and I don't drink much, so it adds up. My dad always said a single guy on a mining wage has no excuse to be broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the AI tool on your cycle times, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I film a few loads from the cab with my phone, note the times, and ask it what's different between my fast ones and my slow ones. Usually it's that I'm hesitating on the swing back. Hamid laughed at me, then asked me to show him.

S0.say: I'd say we got better tools and the bubble popped. I'd probably post a chart about it online, but nobody at work would care much.
S0.think: I'd be a bit let down, because I own shares in automation companies. But my job would be safe for longer, so it evens out.
S0.do: Keeps using an AI tool to cut his excavator cycle times and keeps buying shares every month. Still applies to the autonomy project team when it opens.
S0.quote: Hamid laughed at me, then asked me to show him.
S0.fieldNote: Umar treats his own learning like a data project and has money riding on automation. He is hedged both ways: if AI fizzles his job lasts, if it booms his shares do. The story of his shift boss coming round is a small sign of his influence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get on board, not to complain. I'd tell the younger guys to learn the systems now. Online I'd share stuff about what the new jobs actually look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. The excavator will probably still need a person for a while, but the trucks I load will go driverless, and someone has to manage the zone where people and robots meet. I'd want to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first three months I'd apply for the autonomy project team and take any course they offer, even unpaid on my days off. I'd use AI tools every day to learn the fleet management software. I'd keep investing, and I'd put some savings into a short online certificate in industrial control systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. This is the version I'd pick if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might lose out in this picture at your mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck drivers, obviously. Some of them are my mates, like Sione, who's been driving for twelve years. I'd try to drag him along to the courses, but he'd say he's too old for screens at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it fair that you'd do well and they wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not totally, no. But the company should pay for the training on work time, and the government should help people who can't move. Some of it's on the person too. I'm somewhere in the middle on that.

S1.say: I'd say it's time to get on board, not to complain. I'd tell younger workers to learn the systems and share what the new jobs look like online.
S1.think: I think it's good for me, because someone has to manage the zone where people and driverless trucks meet. I'd want to be that person.
S1.do: Applies for the autonomy project team within three months and takes every course, even unpaid on days off. Learns the fleet management software with AI tools and pays for an online certificate in industrial control systems.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, as this is the version he'd choose.
S1.quote: Someone has to manage the zone where people and robots meet.
S1.fieldNote: He moves first and enjoys it. His centrist view splits responsibility between company, government and the individual. His friendship with an older truck driver gives the scenario a human cost he doesn't ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shock and governments need to move fast on income support, because most people can't adjust in two years. At work I'd try to keep people calm. Online I'd be reading more than posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think even the autonomy job only lasts a year or two. If AI can do anything, it doesn't need a guy in a high-vis vest standing between the robots and the people, because there won't be people. My shares would probably go up, which is a strange thing to be grateful for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the job as long as it paid, and get onto the autonomy team so I'd be among the last on site. I'd keep a lot more cash than usual, maybe a year and a half, and leave the shares alone. And I'd look hard at what kinds of work need a human face, because I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I've got money and I'm young, but I don't have a next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' warning, what would you do differently in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard at being useful to the rollout, because those are the last jobs to go. Two years isn't enough for a degree or a trade, so there's no point starting one. I'd rather be inside the change, getting paid, than sitting in a classroom for something that's already gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your shares would go up. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit weird. I'd be making money from the thing that took Sione's job. I'd probably give some of it to my family, my sister's got two kids and her husband drives a truck too.

S2.say: I'd say it's a huge shock and governments must move fast on income support, because most people can't adjust in two years. At work I'd try to keep people calm.
S2.think: Even the autonomy job would only last a year or two, because there won't be people to manage. My shares would probably rise, which is a strange thing to be grateful for.
S2.do: Stays in the job and joins the autonomy team to be among the last on site. Raises his cash reserve to about eighteen months, leaves his shares invested, and looks for work that needs a human face.
S2.feel: Uneasy, with money and youth on his side but no clear next step.
S2.quote: I'd be making money from the thing that took Sione's job.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest picture his savings and investments keep him steady. What unsettles him is not money but direction, and a slight guilt at profiting while friends lose out. He plans to share gains with his family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, so people need to start learning now, and governments need a plan for income before it lands. I'd say the same at work. I'd probably organise a little study group in the crib room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is my sweet spot. I'd get on the autonomy team, get good at the systems, and maybe move into commissioning, which is setting the machines up at new mines. That's work you can sell to lots of mines for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd finish the control systems certificate and get onto the autonomy team. In year two or three I'd look at commissioning work with an equipment supplier, even if it meant travelling. I'd keep investing every month and keep a year of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's fast but I can see the steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A career move instead of a holding pattern. In two years I'm just the last guy in the pit. In five I can become one of the people who installs this stuff at other mines, and I'd be paid well for it while it's being rolled out everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when it arrives, in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm thirty-two with savings, shares and five years of experience in the hottest field going. I don't know what comes after. But I'd be in better shape than most to figure it out.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short, so people should start learning now and governments need an income plan. I'd probably set up a study group in the crib room.
S3.think: Five years is my sweet spot. I'd get onto the autonomy team and maybe move into commissioning, setting machines up at new mines.
S3.do: Finishes his control systems certificate and joins the autonomy team in the first year. Looks at commissioning work with an equipment supplier in year two or three, keeps investing monthly and holds a year of cash.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, seeing clear steps despite the speed.
S3.quote: In two years I'm just the last guy in the pit.
S3.fieldNote: He sees the five-year window as the best for him personally: long enough to build a career out of installing automation. He is honest that he doesn't know what comes after. He'd still help others with a study group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. At work I'd tell everyone to pick something and start learning, because ten years goes fast. Online I'd share courses and tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel great about this one. Ten years is long enough to build real skills and real savings. I'd be thirty-seven and probably working on the machines that do my old job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep digging and get on the autonomy team when it opens. I'd start a part-time diploma in electrical or mechatronics, which is mechanical plus electronics plus computing. And I'd keep investing, because ten years of monthly investing is serious money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a long, good runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about in the ten-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable. Ten years sounds long, and I've seen guys say they'll study next year for a decade. I'd need to set myself deadlines, probably with the AI tool nagging me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything in your personal life change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd buy a place instead of renting, because I'd feel safe enough. And maybe settle down, my mum keeps asking. But I wouldn't do that in the two-year version, I'd want the cash.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. I'd tell everyone at work to pick something and start learning, and share courses online.
S4.think: I'd feel great about this one, with time to build real skills and savings. At thirty-seven I'd probably be working on the machines that do my old job.
S4.do: Keeps digging and joins the autonomy team when it opens. Starts a part-time mechatronics diploma and keeps investing every month for the full ten years.
S4.feel: Calm, like having a long, good runway.
S4.quote: I've seen guys say they'll study next year for a decade.
S4.fieldNote: The decade-long picture is the most comfortable for him, and his main fear is getting complacent. Extra time also opens up personal plans like buying a home. He clearly ties big life choices to how much warning there is.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to build anything, you just ride it out. What would help is the company being honest early about the timeline, and some kind of income support that doesn't punish people for having saved. I'd also like proper short courses that are actually about the machines on our site.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want to stay in mining. I would, actually. I like the dirt and the size of everything, and I'd rather be the guy fixing the robot excavator at five in the morning than writing code in a city office.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the guy fixing the robot excavator at five in the morning than writing code in a city office.
portrait: Umar Santos is a 27-year-old trainee excavator operator at a large lithium mine, still slower than his crewmates and using an AI tool every night to study his own cycle times. He lives alone, has about nine months of cash and a share portfolio worth another year, much of it in automation companies. He stays calm in most pictures and sees the steady and five-year versions as chances to move into the autonomy team and commissioning work. Only the two-year AGI picture leaves him uneasy, more for lack of direction and guilt about friends than for money.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to build anything and he would just have to ride it out.
whatWouldHelp: Early honesty from the company about timelines, income support that doesn't punish savers, and short courses on the actual machines on site.
